topComments.author: Pannoniae
topComments.text: Nice article :) Yeah this is basically a tradeoff between CPU and GPU power. There are different types of culling. There's the basic stuff like backface culling (supported in hardware, don't render triangles facing away from you) and frustum culling (don't render objects which your camera doesn't see). These are used in just about every game. For occlusion culling it's a bit more tricky because you can either do it on the CPU in broadly two ways, either do low-res raycasting / software rendering like in the article on the CPU and cull based on that. This is an adaptive workload, you can give it more threads or CPU power and it scales for better culling which results in less pixels rendered on the GPU. You can also use GPU culling but that's more complicated to do and that uses the GPU which creates a catch-22 - you want to use GPU culling to reduce GPU load but integrated GPUs don't cope well with compute shaders and memory bandwidth in general, so doing a culling pass might wipe out any culling gains you might have. And dedicated GPUs have the raw power and memory bandwidth to just submit everything in your frustum and get most of it depth-rejected. I wonder if it would be even faster to create a connectivity graph on the CPU, like each chunk knows whether a neighbour is visible and vice versa. On rendering the chunk graph is walked and the visible chunks are submitted, kind of like a primitive garbage collector to determine liveness. The culling would be worse but I presume traversing a fairly small (few thousand elements) list is quite a bit cheaper than rendering the "mipped" occlusion boxes, but do let me know if this is wrong.

stories.title: Show HN: Jevstiller – Distill Jev into a local model, with a disagreement bound
stories.author: tgluck

topComments.author: tgluck
topComments.text: Author here. This puts a proxy in front of repeated Jev classification calls. At first everything goes to Jev; from Jev's answers it trains a small head on frozen sentence embeddings, picks a confidence threshold with an exact finite-sample bound so that at most 2% of all requests get an answer Jev wouldn't have given, and then answers the confident share locally at ~15 ms on a CPU. A permanent 2% audit keeps checking; if agreement breaks, everything falls back to Jev and it retrains. Known limits: agreement is not accuracy (if Jev is wrong, so is the local model); coverage tracks how consistent Jev itself is (22% on noisy tweet tasks, 80% on news); it speaks Jev's API only, an OpenAI-compatible front is on the roadmap. Since 0.4.0 the guarantee can also cover "would Jev have been unsure", which matters if your code routes low-confidence answers to review. Apache 2.0.

jobs.text: We're the system of record for the Canadian vehicle: raw automotive data turned into facts that can be checked. Our open-source VIN decoder sits underneath a government vehicle registry. stackOverflowQuestions.title: How do I manage Mongock / Flamingock data migrations with a rolling Kubernetes deployment?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: We use kubernetes to deploy our services, and our services typically have three or more replicas. This has caused a problem when we want our Spring Boot-initialized Mongock (and soon, Flamingock) to perform any data migration: when performing a normal roll-out, the change unit will be performed by the first upgraded pod rather than the last one. Example Quick example why this is a problem: We've designed the new version of the code (B) to work appropriately with the old version of our Mongo documents (1). We've designed the new version of the data (2) to be compatible with the old code (A) during our transition period. We've written the Mongock change unit to convert all of the documents from version (1) to version (2). What would happen if we did it naively: Pod (a) deploys and runs the change unit. All data is updated to version (2). Pods (b) and (c) continue writing data in version (1). Pod (b) and (c) update. They see that the change unit has already been run, and skip it. The collection is left with almost all documents updated to version (2), but with those few new documents from pods (b) and (c) in version (1). In practice, this has led us to not use Mongock change units to perform migrations. However, this seems like a problem that should have a solution. Solutions We've Considered Scale down the service to 0 before the update. With our current CI setup, this is a bit of a challenge, but we've performed these steps when needed. Have the idempotent change unit run every time. This is against the spirit of Mongock, but would technically work. Unlike other solutions, this one encourages removing the change unit after it's been run. Trigger the change unit via some external event, like an endpoint. I haven't figured out how to externally trigger a single Mongock change unit, and it's (again) against the spirit of Mongock, but this could work. However, they have an argument name mismatch ( obj vs item ): # in multiprocessing.Queue: def put(self, obj, block=True, timeout=None): ... # in queue.Queue: def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... So if I try to make them both SupportsPut s, I can only choose either obj or item as the abstract argument: class SupportsPut(Protocol): def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... def do_something_with(thing: SupportsPut): pass do_something_with(mp.Queue()) # <- do_something_with(q.Queue()) I get as expected a Pylance error that mp.Queue.put doesn’t conform to the protocol’s put . But I don’t know how to let the protocol method know that. This is just an example of the “slight difference in function signature” I mentioned. Maybe one implementation offers more kwargs than the other; maybe one has / or * specifiers; maybe one has an argument with a narrower type; etc. In most of these cases the difference can be worked around by the user function do_something_with by calling the methods in a specific way as shown above.
